finding: Per the NYT report, 'Shape of You' began from a Steve Mac keyboard riff about 15 minutes into the session, and Sheeran stacked parts one by one the way he does live with a looper. McDaid says Sheeran was firing melodies almost at once. The reporter says the melodies started as wordless syllables, with the lyric developing later. Because the chord loop barely changes, McDaid says they used dynamics, lyric and rhythm to make the sections differ. In 2023 trial testimony reported by AP (ST-S32 paras 3, 5), Sheeran separately described singing in his own 'phonetics' first, after which the words follow.
quote: Within 30 seconds Ed was firing melodies out
why_it_matters: When the loop is fixed, write the vocal rhythm and vowel shapes first in syllables, then let words settle into the stresses already set, and get section contrast from rhythm and density rather than new chords.
when_not: Rhythm-first syllables can leave a lyric that only fits the groove; McDaid's chorus objection (ST-F3) shows the words still needed a meaning check afterwards.

source: ST-S29#answer to the 'yin and yang' question; answer on starting sessions
finding: Johnny McDaid (Music Week, 29 Sep 2026) calls himself the slow one and Sheeran the fast one in their partnership. He says Sheeran produces a constant flood of ideas, and that McDaid's own job is to guard the few that feel precious. He says Sheeran can hold intro, pre-chorus, chorus, verse and outro in his head at once, while McDaid works on one section at a time in close detail. McDaid also says he arrives with no prepared starts, and he values the risk of starting from nothing.
why_it_matters: A high-volume room works when one person generates and holds the whole shape while another protects the best fragments and works them in close detail. A tool can support both roles: fast capture, and marking the keepers.
when_not: McDaid warns against reducing the partnership to this contrast; the roles are tendencies, not fixed jobs.

finding: McDaid says that in the original draft, the chorus phrase standing on its own, with nothing before or after it, felt objectifying to him. He suggested the title phrase could carry a wider meaning, the shape of who a person is, rather than only their body. Wikipedia's account (ST-S31, Writing) agrees that the chorus was changed after McDaid's objection.
why_it_matters: A hook phrase that works rhythmically can still say the wrong thing on its own, so check the title line out of context and widen its meaning without changing its sound.
when_not: The fetched sources do not record the discarded wording, so the exact change cannot be studied; do not reconstruct it.

source: ST-S18#Sheeran Instagram statement quoted mid-article (NME, 4 Apr 2025)
finding: Sheeran says he wrote 'Azizam' after Ilya Salmanzadeh suggested making music drawn from Ilya's Persian heritage, and that he wanted a party atmosphere. He says the rhythms, scales, melodies and instruments felt like Irish traditional music, so the song felt familiar despite being new to him. The title is a Persian endearment ('my dear') used as a one-word hook, and NME notes the rest of the lyric is in English. In an NPR interview (ST-S50) Sheeran said he wanted an approach that might work globally.
quote: different but similar to the Irish trad music
why_it_matters: A writer can enter an unfamiliar idiom through the part of it that matches their own roots (here, Irish trad phrasing), which keeps the vocal natural while the setting changes.
when_not: Familiarity can mean the new idiom never goes past the surface. See the critique in ST-F5.

source: ST-S17#Critical reception (summarising Petridis, Guardian 4 Apr 2025; original blocked as ST-S54)
finding: As summarised on Wikipedia, Alexis Petridis argues that the Persian element sits mainly in a chorus counter-melody while the rest is Anglo. He likens the song's relation to Persian music to how 'Galway Girl' relates to sean-nos singing. Mark Beaumont (Independent via AOL, ST-S19 paras 1, 3-4) says the English lyric reads like a weak machine translation and treats the single as commercial strategy, though he rejects the appropriation charge. 'Sapphire' places its second language differently: Arijit Singh sings on the bridge and the song mixes English and Punjabi (ST-S21). Reviews of it split, from best track on the album (BBC) to banal love-song lyrics (Independent) and heavy-handed (Pitchfork).
why_it_matters: Decide on purpose where a borrowed idiom lives: a title word, a counter-melody, a guest bridge or the lyric's own thinking. Critics treat it as decoration unless it reaches the words.
when_not: Both songs did well commercially: Azizam debuted at No. 3 on the UK Singles Chart (week not given in ST-S17), and NPR (ST-S50) says Sapphire went to No. 1 in India (chart and week unnamed). A surface fusion can still connect with listeners.

source: ST-S24#paragraphs on the phone's memories and emotional impact (Fallon appearance, 28 Mar 2025)
finding: Sheeran says 'Old Phone' came from a real object. It was a phone he had put away in 2015, and he switched it back on to supply evidence in a copyright lawsuit. He says it held messages from two friends who had since died, an argument with an ex, and contact from an estranged relative. Malay Mail (ST-S25 paras 8-10) adds that the first message was from the late Jamal Edwards. Unlike the Play singles written with co-writers, the song credits Sheeran alone (ST-S27).
why_it_matters: A physical object that holds dated, unedited evidence gives a verse its concrete details, and it gives the chorus a time-travel angle without stating the theme.
when_not: No fetched source says how the lyric was drafted (Songfacts' claim that he wrote it alone at 2am in India has no source), so the origin is documented but the craft process is not.

finding: At the CHROMAKOPIA listening event, Tyler said the record began as being about growing up in Hawthorne and Inglewood. He said it struck him that nobody knew anything about his life before he was 17, and that only at 33 did his mother's childhood advice make sense. He framed the writing as what he thinks about when alone. He told fans the second listen is when it hits, and the reporter notes he left the album's central concept unexplained.
quote: write about stuff I think about when I'm dolo'ing
why_it_matters: A gap in what people know about you (here, life before 17) can be a concept in itself. Leaving the frame unexplained asks the listener to do the second listen.
when_not: Dork's critic (via ST-S35) says the St. Chroma character shapes the visuals but barely touches the lyrics, so a persona frame can turn into packaging only.

source: ST-S37#section 'Tyler, The Empathic Storyteller' and 'Tyler, The Ambivalent' (Setaro, 28 Oct 2024)
finding: Press describes 'Hey Jane' as a conversation about an unplanned pregnancy with an older partner. Tyler raps both sides, each with its own voice, and the song ends unresolved. Complex (ST-S38 para 5) hears Tyler's half as letter-like, says the partner's reply hits harder, and describes the backing as stripped synths with a relentless metronome-like pulse (text description only, not heard). 'Like Him' (ST-S42; ST-S37 'Tyler, The Son') uses a related shape: the son asks his mother whether he resembles his absent father, and her own recorded voice answers in the outro.
quote: Tyler raps from both perspectives perceptively and empathetically.
why_it_matters: Giving the other person a full verse of their own, not a summary in the narrator's mouth, turns a confession into a scene. Letting the second voice land harder keeps the narrator from winning.
when_not: Slant (ST-S41 para 6) finds the Hey Jane sequence sincere but sanitised and insular, with self-critique that never turns outward, so two voices do not guarantee real stakes.

source: ST-S37#section 'Tyler, The Empathic Storyteller' / 'Tyler, The Ambivalent'
song: Take Your Mask Off — Tyler, the Creator
finding: Press describes each verse of 'Take Your Mask Off' as a portrait of someone living behind a false front: a drama student posing as a gang member, a closeted priest, and a housewife who has given up her identity. Each verse closes by addressing the listener directly with the hope that they drop the mask. The last verse turns the charge on Tyler himself, his selfishness and career anxiety, which Complex (ST-S38 para 7) reads as self-hatred and calls the album's spiritual cornerstone. Credits add Kathryn Thomas and Gregory Cook to Tyler (ST-S35).
why_it_matters: A verse can be a portrait of a stranger with the same closing address each time, so the chorus works as a verdict. Saving the narrator for the final portrait turns the verdict on him.
when_not: Slant (ST-S41 para 2) calls the song's take on its characters simplistic and patronising, a risk whenever character sketches exist mainly to deliver a moral.

finding: Treble praises Tyler's comic wordplay and says the starkly reflective moments give the record its weight, with the two running side by side. NME (ST-S40 para 4) says his lyrical dexterity gives his self-reflection humour and humanity. Complex (ST-S38 paras 6-7) says the showier, funny tracks such as the confrontational 'Thought I Was Dead' keep the album entertaining while the darker story runs underneath. None of the fetched reviews analyses internal rhyme or rhythmic density in detail.
quote: Tyler's talent is undeniable when it comes to slinging humorous wordplay
why_it_matters: Humour placed near a confession keeps the confession from sounding self-pitying, and it earns the listener's trust before the hard line.
when_not: NME's standfirst calls the messaging confused, and Slant (ST-S41) calls the messiness a shield against criticism of half-baked lyrics. Mixing tones can hide a weak idea as easily as it softens a hard one.

source: ST-S44#Zane Lowe quotes section (Mier, Rolling Stone, Aug 2025)
finding: Tyler told Zane Lowe that after CHROMAKOPIA's weight lifted he wanted to be silly again, with inside jokes and outrageous talk as the main goal. He said he set a rule of no intros, outros or bridges and wanted to get to the point, and that he was not trying to be good, precious or innovative. In the same interview (Complex, ST-S45) he says artists build their own handcuffs chasing innovation and that he wants to make and release music the way he did at 17, while admitting the view may be hypocritical. He posted (Clash, ST-S47) that the album was not a concept record. DON'T TAP THE GLASS (released 21 Jul 2025, 10 tracks, 28:30) was made on tour (ST-S48).
quote: No intros, no outros, no bridges.
why_it_matters: A stated rule that removes sections forces every idea to arrive inside the verse and hook. The same writer can alternate a heavily framed record with a deliberately unframed one.
when_not: Rolling Stone's review (quoted in ST-S44) calls it an entertaining pit stop, and The Line of Best Fit (via ST-S43) says it amends existing soil rather than breaking new ground. The no-frills rule trades reach for speed.

finding: Kahan says he wrote the 'Stick Season' chorus on the morning of 29 October, after the posted verse had caught on. He kept the verse's chords because he felt a folk song should stay simple. He sang the chorus's opening line in a country twang, and says that made it much easier to write because it took him out of himself. The song was built in public piece by piece: verse posted, then chorus posted, then a second verse after fans asked for it. In Rolling Stone (ST-S3 para 4) he says the early approval meant he no longer felt forced to finish the chorus.
quote: It felt like I was outside of myself for a second.
why_it_matters: Singing a draft in a borrowed voice or accent can get past self-consciousness and give the chorus a different stance from the verse, even with the same chords.
when_not: Releasing a half-song for approval worked here, but Kahan also links that need for outside validation to insecurity, not to craft.

source: ST-S3#paragraphs 5-6 (Kahan via Rolling Stone Twitch interview)
finding: Kahan says he feared that writing so specifically about Vermont would alienate listeners elsewhere, and was gratified that something so particular to his life connected. On Song Exploder (ST-S1, final-chorus and second-verse sections) he says one late line came straight from living in Strafford after his friends had left. He says the second verse, about his father's depression and his own inherited depression and anxiety, took several days over Thanksgiving, and he included it because the discomfort might help someone. 'Stick Season' itself is local slang for the bare stretch between autumn and winter (ST-S1 opening; ST-S4).
quote: something that was specific to my life
why_it_matters: A place-name or local term the writer worries outsiders won't know can carry the feeling better than a general word, provided the emotion around it is plain.
when_not: The fetched sources record only Kahan's own sense that it connected; they do not test whether the regional term or the family detail did the work.

source: ST-S1#second verse into final chorus (gang-vocal discussion)
finding: Kahan says that after the second verse he wanted another lift from harmonies, and he calls that one of his favourite moments. For the last chorus he recorded gang vocals with Gabe Simon and engineer Konrad Snyder so it would sound like his friends were back home, acting out the lyric's wish. The people he played it to said it might be a little corny (the fetched transcript text does not clearly say who 'they' were). He agreed, and says there was a more nuanced way to do it.
why_it_matters: A last chorus can get its lift from a harmony or texture change rather than new words. Staging the lyric's wish literally (the friends actually singing) can tip from moving into corny.
when_not: The transcript does not make clear how much of the gang vocal survived, so treat this as a decision about tone, not a measured result.

source: ST-S6#early section after demo verses (Song Exploder ep. 151, 8 Jan 2019)
song: Nina Cried Power — Hozier (stand-in; no Too Sweet writer source found)
finding: Hozier says the verses of 'Nina Cried Power' sat as rough early ideas for a long time while he tried to find a reason for the song. He worried it was too soap-boxy and nearly dropped it. The chorus came together once he decided to name artists who had stood up for causes, a roll-call rather than an argument. He justified the directness by pointing to Woody Guthrie and Joni Mitchell. This is the only Hozier Song Exploder episode, and no fetched source holds a Hozier statement on how 'Too Sweet' (2024) was written.
quote: It's too soap-boxy. No one wants to hear this.
why_it_matters: When a message song starts to preach, swap the argument for concrete names or examples. The listener draws the conclusion, and the chorus stops explaining.
when_not: This is a protest song by Hozier alone, so it says little about the playful two-character set-up of 'Too Sweet', which was co-written by a seven-person team.

source: ST-S15#answers on song origin, writing method, and too-personal lyrics (LeDonne, GRAMMY.com, 8 Apr 2024)
finding: Boone says that soon after moving to LA, with only a mattress and a piano, he wrote a verse one sleepless night and a separate chorus idea the next night. A collaborator suggested joining the two, and they then worked on it for a long time (Wikipedia, ST-S51, names Jack LaFrantz as the one who proposed the merge, and credits LaFrantz and producer Evan Blair as co-writers). He writes at the piano late at night and lets his voice lead. He calls vulnerability the most important thing in songwriting, but says he never names or reveals private details about other people.
quote: I let my voice lead where the song goes
why_it_matters: A verse and a chorus written apart can be joined when the tension between them (quiet doubt against a big declaration) is the song. Confessional writing can keep its rawness while staying silent on other people's private details.
when_not: Boone does not discuss the bridge or the last chorus in the fetched interview, and the Billboard and Variety interviews that might have covered them failed to load.
